description.en:
A concise topic-wise e-book covering ancient, medieval and modern Indian history for competitive exams — Indus Valley Civilisation, the Mauryan and Gupta empires, the Delhi Sultanate and Mughals, and the rise of nationalism leading to Independence.

This is an online reading e-book only. It cannot be downloaded as a PDF.

title.en: Indus Valley to the Mauryan Empire

content.en:
The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation flourished around 2500–1750 BC in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent. Its major cities were Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal, Dholavira and Kalibangan. The Harappans were the first to use burnt bricks and had an excellent underground drainage system, but the script is still undeciphered.

In the Vedic age, society was organised into four varnas and the Vedas — Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva — were composed. The later Vedic period saw the rise of large kingdoms called Mahajanapadas, and two new religions, Jainism (founded by Vardhamana Mahavira) and Buddhism (founded by Gautama Buddha), spread across north India.

The first great empire of India was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, guided by his minister Chanakya (Kautilya), the author of the Arthashastra. The Mauryan empire reached its zenith under Emperor Ashoka, who after the Kalinga war embraced Buddhism and spread the policy of Dhamma through his rock and pillar edicts.

The Gupta empire (c. 320–550 AD) is known as the Golden Age of ancient India. Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) ruled at its height, and scholars like Aryabhata, the mathematician-astronomer, and Kalidasa, the great Sanskrit poet, adorned the court. The cave paintings of Ajanta belong to this broad period of cultural efflorescence.

After the decline of the Guptas and Harsha, north India broke into smaller states, and in 1206 the Delhi Sultanate was established by Qutb-ud-din Aibak. The Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties ruled from Delhi. Alauddin Khilji introduced market control reforms and defeated the Mongols, while Muhammad bin Tughlaq is remembered for his ambitious but failed projects such as the transfer of the capital to Daulatabad and the introduction of token currency.

title.as: মোগল, ব্ৰিটিছ শাসন আৰু স্বাধীনতা সংগ্ৰাম

content.en:
The Mughal empire was founded by Babur after the Battle of Panipat in 1526. The empire reached its peak under Akbar, who followed a policy of religious tolerance and administrative centralisation, and later under Shah Jahan, the builder of the Taj Mahal. Aurangzeb's long and costly wars weakened the empire, paving the way for the Marathas and, later, the Europeans.

The British East India Company first came as traders, then became rulers after the Battle of Plassey (1757) and the Battle of Buxar (1764). The Revolt of 1857, the first major war of independence, ended with the British Crown taking direct control of India in 1858.

The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Under Mahatma Gandhi the movement took a mass character through the Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930) and Quit India (1942) movements. Subhas Chandra Bose raised the Indian National Army, and finally India became free on 15 August 1947, though the country was partitioned into India and Pakistan.

Key points to remember:
- Babur founded the Mughal empire at Panipat in 1526.
- Akbar is known for religious tolerance and mansabdari administration.
- Battle of Plassey (1757): British victory over Siraj-ud-daulah.
- Revolt of 1857 ended with Queen Victoria becoming Empress of India.
- INC founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume.
- India attained independence on 15 August 1947.
